  "area": "Computational and circuit complexity",

  "formal": "Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.",
  "definitions": "A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\\in L\\iff\\exists y\\in\\{0,1\\}^{\\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove P=NP or P≠NP. A polynomial-time SAT algorithm settles the equality direction. For separation, prove that some language in NP has no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm; equivalently, rule out every such algorithm for SAT. Failure of a particular search procedure or a lower bound for a restricted circuit model does not establish that separation.",
  "context": "A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.\n\nNP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.\n\nThe two possible answers have different practical limits. P=NP would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. P≠NP would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.\n\nMany successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. They guide the search for new arguments; they are not proofs that the problem is unsolvable.",

  "formal": "Is there a uniform quantum-LOCAL algorithm that, for every n≥3 and every identifier assignment to an n-cycle, outputs a proper 3-coloring with global probability at least 1−1/n in $T(n)=o(1+\\log^* n)$ communication rounds? Every node is given n, its own identifier from [n²], and a consistent clockwise/counterclockwise orientation. Initial quantum registers are unentangled across nodes.",
  "definitions": "The network is a simple cycle; the orientation only identifies predecessor and successor, and communication is allowed in both directions. Nodes do not receive their numerical position in the cycle, a leader, or the list of other identifiers. They run one finite classical control program which may perform arbitrary finite local quantum computations, then exchange finite but unbounded numbers of qubits with each neighbor in each synchronous round. For a concrete uniform model, local quantum operations are finite circuits over H, T, and CNOT, fresh |0⟩ ancillas, and computational-basis measurements with adaptive classical control. Register size, message size, and local computation time are not charged, but are finite on every branch. Initially the joint quantum state is a product of local |0⟩ registers; the given classical local input may affect subsequent operations. No shared randomness, initial entanglement, or graph-dependent advice is supplied. The protocol may generate entanglement by sending qubits during its counted rounds. Every node eventually outputs one color in {1,2,3}. Success means that every cycle edge has differently colored endpoints, simultaneously. T(n) bounds all branches of the protocol, not its expected time. The little-o condition is T(n)/(1+log* n)→0 as n→∞; log* counts iterated base-2 logarithms down to at most 1. This card fixes the standard directed-cycle input variant, while allowing communication in either direction.",
  "answer_criterion": "Construct such a protocol with a proof of its worst-case round bound and global success probability, or prove that no such protocol exists. A constant-round protocol would answer yes. An anonymous zero-error lower bound, a two-color lower bound, or a lower bound using unbounded-degree trees does not by itself answer this high-probability three-color cycle question.",
  "context": "A cycle is the simplest network in which many nearby choices must be coordinated. Two colors encode a global parity constraint, but three colors allow a much more local solution. In classical distributed computing, the exact deterministic cost of this symmetry breaking is Θ(log* n).\n\nNaor’s lower bound shows that classical randomization with high-probability correctness still needs Ω(log* n) rounds. Quantum messages can create correlations unavailable to classical messages, but a coloring algorithm still has to return ordinary classical colors. The question is whether those correlations allow neighboring processors to agree on a valid local pattern faster than the classical symmetry-breaking threshold. The orientation and identifiers are explicit inputs, so no lower bound may rely on their absence.\n\nThere is a fundamental obstacle to arguments based only on causality. Finitely dependent proper colorings exist: far-separated sets of outputs can be independent while all adjacent colors differ. Consequently, the output distribution of a hypothetical constant-round quantum coloring algorithm need not violate a general no-signaling or finite-dependence constraint. Existence of such a distribution does not provide a quantum protocol that samples it.\n\nThe August 2026 result attacks the quantum implementation itself using matrix-product-state structure and a teleportation-based reduction. It proves a linear lower bound for anonymous finite-qubit protocols that must always succeed. Its Section 1.4 explicitly identifies the extension to high-probability correctness as the remaining problem. That is precisely the error regime retained on this card.\n\nA separate July 2026 paper proves a log-star lower bound for 3-coloring rooted trees through growing-degree instances, and a linear lower bound for 2-coloring even cycles. Neither theorem handles the combination here: degree exactly two, three available colors, and small nonzero failure probability.",

  "area": "Data structures and compressed data",
  "criterion": "reductions",
  "formal": "Given a Boolean matrix $M\\in\\{0,1\\}^{n\\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\\ldots,v_n\\in\\{0,1\\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.",
  "context": "If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.\n\nA small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.\n\nThe conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\\Omega(\\sqrt{\\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.\n\nThe graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.",

Set $p=\\mathrm{Select3}(B,\\lceil q/2\\rceil)$. Scan all of A, including its at most two ungrouped final elements, comparing each key with p and forming L of keys below p and R of keys above p, preserving their original order. If k=|L|+1 return p; if k<=|L| return Select3(L,k); otherwise return Select3(R,k-|L|-1). One comparison returns the relative order of two keys at unit cost.   "formal": "For every fixed integer $k\\ge3$, is $\\widetilde\\Omega(n^{1-1/k})$ a worst-case round lower bound for randomized detection of a simple cycle of length exactly 2k in the CONGEST model?   "context": "Cycle detection asks whether information about a bounded number of vertices can be assembled somewhere in the network. With limited messages, a vertex may learn that there are many short paths without having enough information to combine compatible paths into a cycle.\n\nA simple six-cycle uses six distinct vertices. Walking across one edge and back three times is also a closed walk of length six, but is not a valid witness. Conversely, a graph containing a six-cycle may also contain triangles or four-cycles.   "area": "Differential privacy",
  "formal": "Let $Y$ be a finite set of candidates, each with a public loss function $\\ell_y$ of sensitivity one under a one-record database change. To access the database, an algorithm makes $k$ adaptive sensitivity-1 queries. Its answers are $q_i(X)+\\mathrm{Lap}(k)$, where $k$ is the scale. Can it guarantee expected excess loss $O(\\log|Y|)$ for arbitrary losses? The algorithm may choose the number of queries.",
  "context": "This model corresponds to basic composition for pure privacy. The stronger concentration of Gaussian noise cannot simply be transferred.\n\nHere the menu of candidates is finite and each loss changes by at most one when one database record changes. The algorithm tries to choose a candidate whose expected loss is close to the best available loss. Its only observations are sensitivity-bounded statistical queries with Laplace noise.\n\nTaking more queries is not free in this interface: the noise scale of each answer grows with the total query count k. A method that estimates all losses can spend too much accuracy on candidates that will never be selected. A method that repeatedly eliminates candidates risks making irreversible choices from noisy comparisons. The problem asks whether a carefully organized query process can still reach logarithmic excess loss.",

  "formal": "Does there exist a deterministic comparison algorithm and an absolute constant C that, for every legal sequence of N insert and delete-min operations starting from an empty priority queue, determines exactly which inserted items remain after the entire sequence using at most CN key comparisons?   "definitions": "Each insert introduces a distinct item with a key in an opaque totally ordered universe; all inserted keys are pairwise distinct. A delete-min removes the currently present item of smallest key. Legality means that in every prefix the number of delete-min operations is at most the number of inserts. If I is the total number of inserts, the output is an I-bit vector in insertion order, marking exactly the items still present after all N operations. The algorithm may examine any part of the input sequence at any time. Its only access to key values is by pairwise order comparisons; operation positions and item identities carry no information about key order. Count every key comparison, including preprocessing comparisons. Ordinary computation on indices and comparison outcomes is not the cost measure, but the algorithm must terminate and be correct on every input.",
  "answer_criterion": "Give a uniform deterministic algorithm meeting the CN comparison bound for every legal sequence, or prove that every such algorithm requires a superlinear number of comparisons on a family of inputs. Sorting all removed items or simulating the queue online would solve stronger tasks; a lower bound for those stronger tasks is not a negative answer here.",
  "context": "A usual priority queue must identify each minimum when the corresponding request arrives. The offline task can postpone every decision and return only a final set. For example, after insert(8), insert(2), delete-min, insert(1), the survivors are 8 and 1. This is not simply the set of the two largest inserted keys: 2 disappeared before 1 became available. The interleaving still matters even though the intermediate outputs are discarded.\n\nOne upper bound is to simulate a comparison heap and mark its remaining elements, using O(N log(N+2)) comparisons. At the other extreme, when all insertions precede all deletions, one linear-time selection suffices to find the surviving upper part of the key order. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove the stated bound for every fixed positive epsilon, or prove omega>2. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.\n\nThe question is whether one can keep reducing the extra exponent all the way to zero. Its quantifiers matter. An algorithm for each exponent 2+epsilon is enough, even when its constant depends badly on epsilon. Conversely, improving one decimal place in the current upper bound does not establish the conjecture. Fixing the field and counting exact scalar operations also separates this question from approximate numerical multiplication or hardware throughput.\n\nModern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.\n\nThere are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.",

{

  "title": "Is 3-colorability polynomial-time decidable on diameter-two graphs?",
  "area": "Graph theory and graph algorithms",
  "criterion": "decision",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph G of diameter at most 2, decides whether there is a map c:V(G)→{1,2,3} such that c(u)≠c(v) for every edge uv?",
  "definitions": "The input is the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph. Distance counts edges in a shortest path, and diameter is the maximum distance between any two vertices. The graph has no loops or parallel edges. For a singleton the diameter is 0. The algorithm must correctly decide existence of a coloring, including on graphs that are not 3-colorable; it is not supplied with a coloring or a promise of 3-colorability. The color set has fixed size three and there are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, degree bounds, or forbidden-subgraph assumptions. A polynomial-time algorithm has worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for constants C,k independent of G. One may equivalently define a total language that rejects disconnected or diameter-greater-than-two graphs, since the diameter promise can be checked in polynomial time. Restricting to diameter exactly two gives the same polynomial-time question: diameter-zero and diameter-one connected graphs are complete and their colorability is immediate.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove that such an algorithm exists, or that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-completeness proof would establish the conventional hardness classification and imply a negative answer under P≠NP. A subexponential algorithm or an algorithm requiring an additional graph restriction does not settle this question.",
  "context": "The 2019 source discusses several diameter-restricted coloring problems. This card selects its central explicit question, with three colors and diameter two. The same section also asks about triangle-free inputs and about coloring claw-free graphs with an input-dependent number of colors; these are distinct extensions, not additional requirements hidden in this question.\n\nBounding diameter means every pair of vertices is close, but it does not bound the amount of global information encoded by the graph. Diameter-one graphs are complete and trivial to color. Mertzios and Spirakis show that 3-colorability is already NP-complete at diameter three, even for triangle-free graphs. Diameter two is the remaining boundary between these neighboring cases.\n\nA tempting hardness reduction adds a universal vertex to an arbitrary graph. This makes the diameter at most two, but the new vertex consumes a color that none of the old vertices can use. It transfers general 3-colorability to 4-colorability, so it does not prove hardness of the fixed three-color target. Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.\n\nThe best general upper bound identified in the July 2026 source is subexponential: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski give time 2 raised to O(n^(1/3) log² n). Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.\n\nMurakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.",
  "why": "Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.",

  "definitions": "The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. {
  "key": "total_quantum_communication",
  "title": "A polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication for total functions",
  "area": "Communication complexity",
  "formal": "For a total Boolean function $F:X\\times Y\\to\\{0,1\\}$, let $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)$ be public-coin randomized communication complexity and $Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F)$ quantum communication complexity with unlimited shared entanglement. Is there a universal polynomial $p$ such that $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)\\le p(Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F))$ for every total $F$?",
  "context": "Partial functions can exhibit exponential quantum savings. Requiring correctness on every input pair may fundamentally restrict that advantage.\n\nAlice receives x and Bob receives y. They need to compute a function of both inputs while exchanging as little information as possible. The classical protocol may use randomness, and the quantum protocol may begin with shared entanglement. The cost being compared is the communication, not the complexity of their local computation.\n\nTotality means every pair of legal individual inputs must receive a correct answer, including pairs that a promise problem would exclude. A universal polynomial simulation would limit quantum communication savings across all such functions. A bound for a special composition, or one with an additional dependence on the input length, does not automatically supply that universal relation.",

{
  "id": "TCS-0513",
  "title": "Can constant-time LOCAL solvability on unrooted trees be decided?",
  "area": "Distributed and local algorithms",
  "criterion": "decision",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Is there a Turing algorithm D that, given a finite description of a locally checkable labeling problem Π on trees of maximum degree Δ, always halts and decides whether Π has a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that solves every allowed input instance in at most t communication rounds, for some constant t depending only on Π? Trees are unrooted, arbitrary finite input labels are allowed, and each node knows the exact number n of nodes.",
  "definitions": "The input description is (Δ,r,Σ_in,Σ_out,C), with integers Δ≥2,r≥1, finite nonempty input and output alphabets, and a finite list C of permitted rooted radius-r neighborhood types. Neighborhoods record input/output labels, degrees and incident port numbers, but not processor IDs or n. Ports at a degree-d node are numbered 1,…,d; the two port numbers of an edge need not agree. A labeling is valid precisely when every node’s radius-r neighborhood is isomorphic, preserving this data and its center, to a type in C. Instances range over every finite nonempty simple undirected tree of degree at most Δ, every input labeling, and every port numbering. Processors additionally have distinct IDs in {1,…,n²}. Initially a node knows its own input, ID, degree, ports, n, and Π. In each synchronous round it can send arbitrary finite messages to its neighbors; local computation is unrestricted in cost but must be computable and terminate. The same finite program runs at every node and works for all n and all ID assignments. No distinguished global root, parent pointers, randomness, or additional advice is supplied. D itself is centralized, with no running-time bound. Descriptions with an unsolvable instance are no instances of the decision problem.",
  "answer_criterion": "Give an always-terminating decider for exactly the described constant-round solvability property, or prove that no such decider exists. A procedure that eventually recognizes every positive instance but may run forever on negative instances is insufficient. This is an explicitly chosen binary subproblem of the saved broader question about deciding the entire asymptotic complexity.",
  "context": "An LCL is specified by local rules rather than a global objective. Proper coloring and maximal independent set illustrate the distinction: a completed labeling can be checked from small neighborhoods, yet finding a valid labeling may require substantially more communication. Here the input to the decision procedure is the rulebook itself, not one network to label.\n\nThe question asks whether a finite rulebook reveals that a bounded communication radius will always suffice. The radius may be enormous and may depend on the rulebook, but it cannot grow with the network. Testing small trees alone cannot certify this property; a procedure must account for every larger tree, every input labeling, and every assignment of identifiers.\n\nThe possible round complexities and the ability to recognize them are separate issues. Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt prove that an LCL on bounded-degree trees with o(log* n) complexity actually has constant complexity. Their paper nevertheless explicitly leaves constant-time decidability open. A gap theorem supplies a separation between cases without automatically providing a test for which case applies.\n\nPositive instances can be recognized by searching the finite local-rule candidates associated with each fixed radius. If a suitable radius exists, this search eventually finds it. The missing part is a terminating certificate or other method for the negative answer. The full complexity-classification question would also need to distinguish further classes, so an affirmative answer here is only one stage of that larger goal.\n\nRooted-tree classification results use the supplied parent-child direction to organize their certificates. An arbitrary port numbering on an unrooted tree provides no such globally consistent direction. Recent results also show that knowledge of network size and the computability of local state transitions can matter. This card fixes both assumptions rather than silently moving between models.",

splay-deque-conjecture.json:
{
  "title": "Do splay trees support deque operations in constant amortized time?",
  "area": "Data structures and compressed data",
  "criterion": "tightness",
  "formal": "Start from an arbitrary binary search tree containing $n$ ordered keys, and perform $m$ legal double-ended queue operations. Insert-min creates a new minimum as the root with the old tree as its right child; insert-max is symmetric. Delete-min splays the minimum to the root, removes it, and keeps its right subtree; delete-max is symmetric. Is the total number of primitive pointer operations and rotations always $O(n+m)$, with a universal constant? This is Tarjan’s deque conjecture for the specified splay implementation.",
  "context": "A deque allows insertion and deletion at either end of a sequence. A linked representation can implement this abstract interface in constant time per operation. The conjecture concerns what happens when the same interface is implemented by a self-adjusting search tree: it asks whether the tree automatically achieves the linear total cost available for this restricted workload.\n\nDeleting the minimum of a long left spine can require many rotations in a single operation. The real difficulty is to understand whether alternating insertions and deletions at opposite ends can repeatedly rebuild expensive configurations.\n\nFor a concrete contrast, deleting keys in increasing order is a sequential-access pattern.   "context": "Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent.   "definitions": "A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected.   "context": "In two dimensions, a suitable decomposition $M=M_1+M_2$ into column and row codewords must satisfy $|\\mathrm{supp}(M)|\\ge\\rho(n_1|M_1|_{\\mathrm{col}}+n_2|M_2|_{\\mathrm{row}})$.\n\nThe two-dimensional picture separates an array into contributions organized by rows and by columns. {
  "id": "TCS-0469",
  "title": "What is the deterministic round complexity of maximum independent set in the congested clique?",
  "area": "Distributed and local algorithms",
  "criterion": "resources",
  "question_type": "asymptotic_complexity",
  "formal": "Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.",
  "definitions": "There is one processor for each vertex in {1,...,n}. Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\\max\\{1,\\lceil\\log_2 n\\rceil\\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |S| >= |I| for every independent set I of the input graph. Define T_MIS(n) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.",
  "answer_criterion": "Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function f(n), construct protocols taking O(f(n)) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires Omega(f(n)) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.",
  "context": "The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.\n\nA simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take O(n / log n) rounds for n >= 2. Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. {

  "title": "Does NP contain a language without polynomial-size Boolean circuits?",
  "area": "Computational and circuit complexity",
  "criterion": "models",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Is $\\mathrm{NP}\\nsubseteq\\mathrm{P/poly}$? Precisely, does there exist one language L∈NP such that, for every integer k≥1, real C>0, and integer N≥1, some n≥N satisfies $\\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k$, where Lₙ is the characteristic function of L on n-bit inputs and CC is minimum Boolean circuit size?",
  "definitions": "A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n input bits, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants 0 and 1, and one output bit. There are no depth or fan-out restrictions; a gate output may be reused arbitrarily. Size counts AND, OR, and NOT gates. Lₙ must be computed exactly on every n-bit string. A family {Cₙ} is nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct Cₙ from n, and the circuit may depend arbitrarily on the input length, but not on the particular input of that length. P/poly consists of languages having circuits of size at most C(n+1)^k for some fixed constants C,k and every n. NP consists of languages L with a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p such that x∈L iff some y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. The existentially chosen language L is the same for every exponent k. The lower bound need only hold at arbitrarily large lengths for each k; an eventual bound at every sufficiently large length would be stronger. Equivalently, ask whether the NP-complete language SAT has no polynomial-size circuit family under an ordinary explicit binary formula encoding.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove NP is not contained in P/poly, or prove the containment. A positive separation requires one NP language escaping every polynomial circuit-size bound. Proving that, for each exponent k, a possibly different language requires more than n^k gates does not suffice. Containment can be established by giving polynomial-size circuits for SAT at every input length; an efficient uniform circuit generator is not required.",
  "context": "A polynomial-time algorithm yields a polynomial-size circuit for each input length by unrolling its computation. The converse fails because a different circuit may be selected for every length without any effective way to generate those circuits. The conjecture asks whether NP retains hard problems even after granting this substantial extra freedom. A separation would imply P≠NP, while P≠NP alone does not establish the circuit claim.\n\nCounting arguments show that most truth tables need exponentially many gates. They do not produce the required language in NP: an arbitrary sequence of hard truth tables need not have efficiently verifiable membership certificates. This is the central explicitness difficulty. It is also why enumerating hard functions at a few fixed lengths cannot satisfy the quantified statement on this card.\n\nThe Karp–Lipton theorem gives a consequence of the opposite outcome: if NP has polynomial-size circuits, the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level. This is evidence linking nonuniform algorithms to uniform complexity, but it is not a contradiction because the hierarchy is not known to be infinite.\n\nThe natural-proofs theorem identifies a conditional obstacle to a broad family of circuit lower-bound techniques. Under sufficiently strong pseudorandom-function assumptions, a property of truth tables that is both efficiently recognizable and sufficiently common cannot distinguish all hard functions from polynomial-size circuits in the required way. The theorem constrains a method, not every possible proof.\n\nWilliams’ separation for nondeterministic exponential time and constant-depth modular circuits demonstrates that faster satisfiability algorithms can yield nonuniform lower bounds. It leaves two restrictions relative to this target: the hard language may lie above NP, and the competing circuits have constant depth.",
  "why": "This is the main unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound conjecture for efficiently verifiable problems. Circuits remove issues of uniform program construction and expose a finite combinatorial object, making the problem a central route toward unconditional computational lower bounds.   "formal": "Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time?   "answer_criterion": "Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer.   "definitions": "Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word.   "formal": "Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer p>=0, every n>=1, every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map F:S^n -> S^n with coefficients in S? Starting with x^(0)=(0,...,0), perform synchronous iteration x^(t+1)=F(x^(t)). There must exist an integer t<=C(p+1)n with x^(t+1)=x^(t). Here p-stability means $1\\oplus a\\oplus\\cdots\\oplus a^p=1\\oplus a\\oplus\\cdots\\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. This is the grounded polynomial-system formulation of the source’s proposed linear convergence bound.",
  "definitions": "A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times a=0. No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and a^0=1. Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by (p+1)n is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.",
  "context": "In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.\n\nThe stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element.   "why": "The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. {

  "title": "Can an acyclic subgraph preserve a constant fraction of the optimal reachable pairs?",
  "area": "Graph theory and graph algorithms",

  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "For a finite directed graph G=(V,E), let $R(D)=|\\{(u,v)\\in V^2:u\\ne v,\\text{ a directed path from }u\\text{ to }v\\text{ exists in }D\\}|$ and $\\mathrm{OPT}(G)=\\max\\{R((V,F)):F\\subseteq E,\\ (V,F)\\text{ is acyclic}\\}$. Do there exist a constant alpha>0 and a deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in |V|+|E| that, for every G, outputs F subset E with (V,F) acyclic and R((V,F)) >= alpha OPT(G)? The constant and polynomial exponent must be independent of G. This card selects constant-factor approximation as a precise target within the source’s broader optimization question.",
  "definitions": "The input is an adjacency-list representation of an unweighted directed graph with labeled vertices 1,...,n, no self-loops, and at most one edge for each ordered pair. Oppositely directed edges may both be present. The algorithm may delete edges but may not add edges, reverse edges, identify vertices, or remove vertices. Reachability uses paths of positive length and counts ordered pairs of distinct vertices, not paths or retained edges. An acyclic graph has no directed cycle. Output is the list of retained edges. Polynomial time is measured in ordinary bit operations on the finite input; no oracle for reachability or optimization is free. When OPT(G)=0, any acyclic output satisfies the value requirement.",
  "answer_criterion": "Give a polynomial-time algorithm and prove one universal positive approximation ratio, or prove that no algorithm with the quantified guarantee exists. A conditional impossibility result must identify its complexity assumption. Guarantees on the number or weight of deleted edges, or empirical similarity to a reference hierarchy, do not establish the required guarantee on reachable pairs.",
  "context": "A directed edge can represent a declared relation between two concepts, while a path represents an implied relation. Removing one edge can therefore erase many implications even if almost every input edge remains. The objective counts the implications preserved after all cycles have been removed. The optimum in the denominator already obeys acyclicity, so the algorithm is not asked to retain mutually contradictory reachability in both directions.\n\nFor example, a directed path on n vertices has only n-1 edges but n(n-1)/2 reachable ordered pairs. Deleting a middle edge destroys roughly a quarter of all n^2 ordered pairs. Conversely, adding a shortcut between vertices that are already connected by a path increases the edge count without adding a new reachable pair. These examples explain why edge-count approximation guarantees cannot simply be reused for this objective.\n\nAjwani’s 2016 question asks for an acyclic edge subgraph whose transitive closure has maximum size, motivated by cleaning taxonomies assembled from multiple contributors. The source explicitly welcomes approximation algorithms and scalable heuristics but specifies no approximation threshold. The constant alpha target here is an editorial specialization, rather than an approximation conjecture quoted from the seminar.\n\nThe 2017 follow-up on noisy hierarchies develops practical cycle-removal heuristics and evaluates recovery of inserted noisy edges. It identifies deviation in transitive closure as a possible further measure. Those experiments do not provide a worst-case ratio for R(D). A 2026 ranking paper likewise uses reachability to make edge reinsertion cycle-safe, but optimizes edge-weight disagreement; that use of reachability does not turn its objective into this one.",
  "why": "This isolates how much implied relational information can be retained when a cyclic dependency system must become a partial order. It is a structural approximation problem in which the value of an edge depends on all paths that use it, and it asks for a guarantee on that global effect.",

  "context": "Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.\n\nThe challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.\n\nConverting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.\n\nThe July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.",

The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words.   "area": "Data structures and compressed data",

  "formal": "Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let OPT(X) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree T₀ and every X, $\\mathrm{cost}_{\\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\\le C(\\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)$? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.",
  "context": "A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.\n\nThe benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.\n\nFor example, imagine alternating long phases that repeatedly access two different small clusters of keys. A static layout must compromise between the clusters; an adaptive tree can reorganize between phases. The challenge is to pay for reorganization only when it is justified, even when an adversary changes the pattern. This is an illustrative example, not a new lower bound.\n\nThe 2026 analysis compares splaying directly to a moving optimal tree. Its remaining multiplicative factor still grows with n. Removing that factor would establish a universal constant-competitive guarantee, not merely another locality-sensitive upper bound.",

The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\\mathbb E_{x\\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\\varepsilon]\\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial.   "answer_criterion": "Prove or disprove the displayed implication for ordinary Turing computation. A positive answer must derive existence of a pair (L,D) outside the precisely defined AvgP from P≠NP alone. A relativized separation only limits relativizing proof methods.",

{

  "area": "Distributed and local algorithms",
  "criterion": "resources",
  "formal": "Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm that outputs a maximal independent set on every $n$-vertex simple graph in $O(\\log n)$ synchronous communication rounds? Each vertex has a distinct $O(\\log n)$-bit identifier, and the guarantee must hold for every valid identifier assignment and every maximum degree. The output must be independent, and every vertex outside it must have a neighbor inside it. No random bits are available.",
  "context": "Identifiers make deterministic symmetry breaking possible, but they do not automatically make it fast. Consider the rule that selects every vertex whose identifier is smaller than those of all its remaining neighbors, then removes the selected vertices and their neighbors. On a path with identifiers increasing from one endpoint to the other, each phase selects just the smallest remaining endpoint. This rule takes linearly many phases, even though much faster algorithms exist for paths.\n\nRandomized MIS algorithms avoid adversarial identifier patterns by making new random choices. A deterministic algorithm has to arrange useful progress from the graph and identifiers alone. The existence of a good assignment of random choices is insufficient: processors must find suitable choices while paying for the communication that coordinates them.\n\nNetwork decomposition supplied a general way to organize that work into small-diameter clusters that can be processed in groups. It settled the old question of whether polylogarithmic deterministic MIS is possible. The present target concerns the finer exponent and cannot be recorded as the already-solved polylogarithmic-time question.\n\nThe 2024 improvement reaches approximately $\\log^{5/3}n$ rounds and avoids the log-squared cost of the standard decomposition-based route. Closing the remaining gap requires more than optimizing the constants of that route. The 2026 coloring reduction still uses this improved MIS bound as its benchmark.",
  "why": "This measures the quantitative cost of removing randomness from a basic distributed task. I include it separately from randomized sublogarithmic MIS because the algorithm must work against every identifier assignment with no failure probability. An O(log n) result would match the familiar randomized worst-case benchmark and propagate through reductions to other symmetry-breaking problems.",
  "definitions": "LOCAL allows unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. A vertex’s r-round view contains only its radius-r neighborhood and the identifiers and input data revealed there. The complexity is elapsed communication rounds until all vertices output.   "title": "Does general rational linear programming have a strongly polynomial algorithm?",
  "area": "Optimization and mathematical programming",

  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\\min\\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\\ x\\ge0\\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most p(m+n) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most q(N)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.",
  "definitions": "A is in Q^(m by n), b in Q^m, and c in Q^n, with m,n>=1. All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of c^T x is minus infinity.",
  "answer_criterion": "Construct and prove correct an algorithm meeting both the dimension-only operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths for every input, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A bound depending on coefficient length or a condition number is insufficient unless that dependence is eliminated. A lower bound for one pivot rule or one class of interior-point trajectories does not establish nonexistence of all strongly polynomial algorithms.",
  "context": "Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.\n\nBoth requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.\n\nCombinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.\n\nFor unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.",

Does it have an interactive proof with a $\\operatorname{poly}(n)$-time verifier, a $\\operatorname{poly}(T(n))$-time honest prover, and a constant completeness–soundness gap?   "context": "IP = PSPACE alone does not guarantee that producing the proof costs only a polynomial in the original computation time.\n\nInteractive proofs separate the effort of checking a computation from the effort of producing a convincing transcript. {
  "id": "TCS-0474",
  "title": "Can pointer-machine working-set heaps have constant amortized insertion and decrease-key?",
  "area": "Data structures and compressed data",
  "criterion": "models",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Does there exist a deterministic online priority queue in the pointer-machine model below and an absolute constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations, starting from an empty queue, has total cost at most $C(M+\\sum_{x\\ \\mathrm{extracted}}\\log \\Gamma(x))$? The operations are insert, find-min, decrease-key, and extract-min. For an extracted item x, define $\\Gamma(x)=1+$ the number of insertions strictly after x was inserted and before it was extracted, including inserted items that have already been removed. An insertion creates a distinct item and returns its handle; decrease-key receives that handle and its new key. Require exact answers for all sequences; melding is not required.",
  "definitions": "Keys are opaque values in a totally ordered set and can only be compared; ties are broken by a fixed order on item identities. Find-min returns the minimum live item; extract-min also removes it. Decrease-key changes the key of an existing item to a no-larger value and does not reset its insertion time. A pointer machine has records containing O(1) pointers and O(1) auxiliary bits, together with the supplied key records. A fixed program operates through O(1) pointer registers. Charge one step for a key comparison, a pointer traversal or change, a constant-bit operation, or allocation of one constant-size record. It cannot perform address arithmetic or unit-cost operations on an unbounded auxiliary integer; larger counters must be explicitly represented and manipulated. All work between requests is charged. Amortization is over every finite sequence, including sequences leaving items in the queue.",
  "answer_criterion": "Construct one queue meeting the displayed total-cost bound for every sequence, or prove that every queue in this model has sequences with an unbounded ratio between its cost and that budget. Constant decrease-key with a growing insertion cost does not establish the positive answer. Neither does a word-RAM implementation using operations absent from the stated model.",
  "context": "The usual priority-queue guarantee charges for extraction according to the number of stored items. A working-set guarantee instead takes account of how recently the extracted item entered the queue. For example, keep a large collection of expensive items present, repeatedly insert one smaller item, and immediately extract it. Each of these recent items has Gamma equal to one, so the proposed budget charges only a constant per such pair of requests. This illustrates the adaptive behavior that the question asks the implementation to exploit.\n\nFast decreases matter independently of these insertion times. A graph algorithm can discover a better tentative distance for an item that has been waiting for a long time. The interface gives the algorithm a handle to that item, but the queue still has to update the organization used to find its next minimum.   "title": "Is perfect matching in general graphs in deterministic NC?",
  "area": "Graph theory and graph algorithms",
  "criterion": "resources",
  "formal": "Given a simple undirected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, can a deterministic parallel algorithm find a perfect matching, or report that none exists, in $(\\log n)^{O(1)}$ time using $n^{O(1)}$ processors? A perfect matching is a set of pairwise vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex. Equivalently, seek a uniform polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuit family for the search problem. Graphs may contain odd cycles; no bipartition is supplied or promised.",
  "context": "A polynomial-time sequential algorithm is known, so the open issue is the length of the dependency chain after work is spread across many processors. Following one augmenting path after another does not automatically give a polylogarithmic number of parallel steps. The processor bound matters too: solving many possibilities simultaneously is useful only if the total work remains polynomial.\n\nChoosing matching edges independently is dangerous. On a four-cycle, every edge can be excluded while preserving some perfect matching. Removing all four edges at once nevertheless destroys every solution. A parallel construction must coordinate its choices around one compatible matching rather than around separate existence certificates.\n\nGeneral graphs also need more structure than the bipartite case. Two disjoint triangles have an even total number of vertices and admit a fractional assignment of one half to every edge, giving total incident weight one at each vertex. They have no perfect matching. This example shows why degree constraints alone do not describe the general matching polytope; odd vertex sets impose additional conditions.\n\nThe June 2026 bipartite result is a major nearby advance. Its theorem covers bipartite graphs, including polynomially bounded weights. The present card deliberately asks for arbitrary graphs, where the deterministic polynomial-processor target remains unresolved in the checked literature.",
  "why": "I include this because perfect matching is a basic polynomial-time graph problem for which randomization and parallelism interact in a particularly sharp way.   "formal": "For each n >= 2, let $D=(D_1,\\ldots,D_n)$ be uniform on the probability simplex, equivalently Dirichlet(1,...,1).   "definitions": "A full binary tree has exactly two children at every internal node. An ordered tree distinguishes left from right, and the fixed leaf order is the alphabetic constraint. Following left and right edges as bits gives an alphabetic prefix code: no leaf codeword is a prefix of another, and lexicographic codeword order agrees with symbol order. The tree is optimized separately after the probabilities D are realized; the expectation is taken afterward. To sample D, draw n-1 independent uniform points in (0,1), sort them, append endpoints 0 and 1, and take the n successive interval lengths. The weights are positive almost surely. For a fixed D, the cost is the expected number of binary decisions to find a leaf drawn with probabilities D; no random-tree distribution is assumed.",

Bounded redundancy or finite Monte Carlo estimates alone do not settle convergence.",
  "context": "An alphabetic tree preserves the order of the symbols, so a search can branch according to comparisons with boundaries in that order.   "key": "private_selection_gaussian",
  "title": "Optimal private selection using only Gaussian queries",
  "area": "Differential privacy",
  "formal": "For a finite set $Y$, public losses $\\ell_y$ have sensitivity 1 under a one-record change in the database $X$. The only access to $X$ is through adaptive queries $q_i(X)+N(0,1/(2\\rho_i))$, with sensitivity at most 1 and $\\sum_i\\rho_i\\le\\rho$. Can the algorithm output $\\hat y$ satisfying $\\mathbb E[\\ell_{\\hat y}(X)]-\\min_y\\ell_y(X)=O(\\log|Y|/\\sqrt\\rho)$?",
  "context": "The exponential mechanism achieves this error with direct data access. The question is whether noise addition alone can exactly match its guarantee.\n\nThe goal is to select a nearly best candidate from a finite menu. A candidate might be a hypothesis or a model configuration, and its loss is evaluated on a private database. The algorithm needs one good choice; accurately estimating every candidate’s loss can be much more information than the task requires.\n\nThe interface restriction is the substance of the question. The algorithm sees only noisy answers and must split a fixed budget among its queries. Spending less budget on a query increases its Gaussian noise. Adaptively narrowing the candidate set might save information, but later decisions are based on earlier noisy comparisons. The target asks whether that process can lose no asymptotic factor relative to optimal direct selection.",

  "title": "Is Exact Matching on general graphs in deterministic polynomial time?",
  "area": "Graph theory and graph algorithms",
  "criterion": "models",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the input bit length, that decides the following problem? Given a simple undirected graph G on an even number n of vertices, each edge colored red or blue, and an integer $0\\le k\\le n/2$, determine whether G has a perfect matching containing exactly k red edges. The algorithm must be correct on every input. No bipartition is promised, and no randomness or computational hardness assumption is allowed.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove that this decision problem belongs to P, or prove that it does not. A randomized polynomial-time algorithm, an approximation to the red count, or an algorithm restricted to bipartite graphs does not establish the positive answer.",

  "title": "Can grammar random access use O(g log g) bits with logarithmic query time?",
  "area": "Data structures and compressed data",
  "criterion": "resources",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\\log(g+2))$ bits and returns T[i] for any $1\\le i\\le N$ in $O(\\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? Preprocessing must take time polynomial in g and is given G, not an expanded copy of T. The space bound includes every persistent index and any retained grammar. Use the word-RAM model below. The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.",
  "definitions": "A binary straight-line program has ordered variables X_1,...,X_g, one rule per variable, and start variable X_g. A rule is X_j -> 0, X_j -> 1, or X_j -> X_a X_b with a,b < j. All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in O(g log(g+2)) bits. Machine words have $\\Theta(\\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use O(log(N+2)) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.",
  "answer_criterion": "Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.",
  "context": "A grammar rule stores references to smaller pieces, so its two references need only logarithmically many bits in the number of rules. A position in the expanded string can require many more bits. For example, a short chain of doubling rules can describe an exponentially long string. This difference is why a space bound stated in machine words can hide a substantial overhead relative to the grammar encoding.\n\nTo locate a position inside a concatenation, the usual navigation step compares that position with the length of the left expansion. Storing an exact expanded length with every variable is straightforward, but can consume g log N bits. The target asks whether this information can be organized or recovered using a representation comparable in bits to the original grammar, while keeping logarithmic access time.\n\nThe April 2026 encoding result improves the grammar representation and keeps logarithmic query time, but retains a g log N expansion-length term. The authors explicitly distinguish their encoding savings from removing that term. Their observation supports treating the latter as a separate question.\n\nICALP 2026 gives much sharper time-space trade-offs in a broad range of parameters. Its main upper-bound theorem uses a space budget above the g log N scale. Consequently, the optimality statements in that range do not automatically settle the smaller bit budget here. This card fixes logarithmic query time, a binary alphabet, polynomial preprocessing, and explicit workspace rules as a concrete specialization of the seminar’s fewer-auxiliary-bits direction.",
  "why": "Random access is the simplest useful operation on a compressed string. Resolving this target would determine whether the extra address-length information is an inherent price of efficient access or an artifact of current representations, and would make the distinction between compressed bits and machine words precise.",

  "formal": "Let H* have vertex set {a₁,a₂,b,c,d,e₁,e₂} and edge set {a₁b,a₂b,bc,cd,de₁,de₂}.   "definitions": "An induced-minor model is a family of seven nonempty, pairwise disjoint vertex sets Bₓ⊆V(G), indexed by x∈V(H*). Each induced subgraph G[Bₓ] must be connected. For every two distinct x,y, an edge of G joins Bₓ to Bᵧ if and only if xy is an edge of H*. Vertices outside the bags are discarded. Equivalently, H* is obtained by deleting vertices and contracting edges; arbitrary edge deletion is forbidden. Parallel edges and loops created inside contractions are suppressed to obtain a simple graph. The seven pattern vertices are names, not prescribed terminals in G. Bags can have unbounded size. H* is fixed and is not part of the input. The input is an adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph, with no promise of planarity, bounded degree, or exclusion of another induced subgraph. The question asks for membership in P, not the optimal polynomial exponent.",

The branch-set definition makes the exact extra obstruction visible.\n\nFiala, Kamiński, and Paulusma developed algorithms for star-like induced minors in 2012.   "formal": "Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\\in\\{0,1\\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\\ge t$. Each T_j is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.",
  "definitions": "A literal is either x_i or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.",
  "answer_criterion": "Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.",
  "context": "Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from 2^n decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.\n\nThe weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take F=(x AND y) OR ((NOT x) AND z), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment (1,0,1) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.\n\nThere is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.\n\nDynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.",

It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.",

{
  "id": "TCS-0492",
  "title": "Is containment of conjunctive queries under bag semantics decidable?",
  "area": "Database theory and finite model theory",
  "criterion": "decision",
  "question_type": "yes_no",
  "formal": "Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries q_1 and q_2 with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\\!:\\!-A_1,\\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and D(A_j[h]) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.",
  "definitions": "A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function U^r to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.",
  "answer_criterion": "Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.",
  "context": "Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.\n\nFor a minimal example, let q(x) have body R(x), and let r(x) have body R(x),R(x). If R(a) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns m^2. Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as m=2. This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.\n\nFor one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.\n\nThe 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.",
  "why": "Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.",

    "assessed_on": "2026-09-10",
    "reason": "A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries."
  },

  "formal": "For the pure pairing heap defined below, is there a universal constant C such that every legal sequence of M operations starting with empty heaps costs at most $C[M+D(1+\\log N)+K(1+\\log\\log(N+2))]$? The allowed operations are make-heap, insert, find-min, meld, decrease-key, and delete-min. Count comparisons and pointer-machine steps; keys are distinct opaque values in a totally ordered set, compared at unit cost. Handles to the affected items and heaps are supplied.",
  "answer_criterion": "Prove this total-cost bound for the specified algorithm, or construct legal operation sequences for which its ratio to the displayed budget is unbounded. Changing the heap algorithm or obtaining the bound only for a different self-adjusting heap does not establish a positive answer.",
  "definitions": "A heap is one rooted heap-ordered tree whose child lists are ordered from left to right. Linking two roots compares their keys and makes the larger root the leftmost child of the smaller; cut removes a node with its subtree from its parent in constant time. Store O(1) pointers per item, with doubly linked child lists. Make-heap creates an empty tree; find-min returns its root; insert links a singleton to the root; meld links the roots and destroys the old heap handles. Decrease-key changes the supplied key and, if its node is not the root, cuts that node and links its subtree with the remaining root. Delete-min removes the root and scans its children left to right, linking disjoint adjacent pairs; an unpaired last child remains. Winners keep their positions in the root list. Identify its minimum-key remaining root v, remove v from that list, and prepend all other remaining roots in their existing order to the child list of v. The resulting tree is the heap. Use the ordinary constant-time list splice, rather than doing an additional recursive linking pass. All loops, comparisons, pointer accesses, and writes are charged. Logarithms have base two.",
  "context": "A decrease-key call changes an item that is already present. It may execute only a few pointer operations immediately, yet the structural disorder it creates can make later deletions more expensive. Its amortized cost measures this delayed effect. Counting only the instructions inside the decrease-key procedure would miss the question entirely.\n\nThe pure pairing heap simplifies deletion by pairing neighboring roots once and then attaching all survivors beneath the smallest survivor. It does not maintain a rank or balance invariant.
