  "area": "Distributed and local algorithms",
  "criterion": "resources",
  "formal": "In the randomized LOCAL model, does there exist an algorithm that finds a maximal independent set in $o(\\log n)$ rounds on every $n$-vertex simple graph? Its output $I\\subseteq V$ must satisfy $(u,v)\\in E\\Rightarrow\\{u,v\\}\\nsubseteq I$ and $v\\notin I\\Rightarrow N(v)\\cap I\\ne\\varnothing$. The bound must hold uniformly over all maximum degrees $\\Delta\\le n-1$.",
  "context": "A sequential greedy algorithm can scan vertices and select each vertex whose neighbors have not been selected. The difficulty here is distributing those decisions: a processor sits at each vertex and initially sees only local information. After r communication rounds, it cannot have learned anything beyond distance r. Message size and local computation are free in LOCAL, so a lower bound measures the reach of coordination itself.\n\nMaximal means that no further vertex can be added. It does not require the largest possible independent set. For example, on a star, either the center alone or all leaves is a valid answer. The challenge is to choose consistently across a general network, rather than to optimize the number of selected vertices.\n\nDegree-sensitive algorithms achieve $O(\\log\\Delta+\\operatorname{poly}(\\log\\log n))$ rounds. This is already sublogarithmic when the degree is sufficiently small; the unresolved target includes polynomial-degree graphs. Repeatedly making only constant-factor progress leaves a logarithmic running time.\n\nRecent work breaks that pattern on graphs with no cycles of length at most six.   "area": "Graph theory and graph algorithms",
  "criterion": "resources",
  "formal": "Given an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge directed graph and a source $s$, is there a randomized shared-memory parallel algorithm that outputs every vertex reachable from $s$ using $\\widetilde O(n+m)$ total work and $(\\log n)^{O(1)}$ depth, with high probability? Work counts all primitive operations across processors; depth is the longest chain of dependent operations.",
  "context": "A breadth-first search does little total work but exposes only the next frontier after processing the current one. On a directed path, that dependency chain is long. Matrix-based transitive closure can instead exploit massive parallelism, but it computes reachability for every pair and may do far more work than one-source search needs. The target asks for the useful properties of both approaches in one algorithm.\n\nThe size of the input and the size of its transitive closure are very different parameters. A one-way path has only $n-1$ edges but $\\Theta(n^2)$ reachable ordered pairs. Thus an algorithm whose work is nearly linear in the closure size can still be quadratic in the input size. This remains true even though the requested one-source answer has only $n$ bits.\n\nShortcuts are a natural way to shorten dependencies: add an edge only when its endpoints were already connected by a directed path, then search the augmented graph. Constructing and storing these edges costs work too. Bounds on what a particular shortcut representation can achieve should not be mistaken for lower bounds on every parallel reachability algorithm.\n\nThe August 2026 result improves the polylogarithmic-depth side of the tradeoff using the size of the transitive closure as a parameter. It is relevant progress, but does not supply near-linear input work on all graphs. This distinction is essential when reading the phrase “faster than transitive closure.”",
  "why": "I include this because reachability is one of the simplest linear-time sequential graph tasks, yet obtaining fast parallel time without wasting substantial work remains difficult. The two-resource formulation makes the goal precise: a faster wall-clock computation should not require polynomially more total computation.",

  "formal": "Over the field $\\mathbb C$, do there exist constants C,k such that, for every integer n≥1, the polynomial $\\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\\sum_{\\sigma\\in S_n}\\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\\sigma(i)}$ can be computed by an arithmetic circuit with at most C(n+1)^k gates? Equivalently, is $\\mathrm{VP}_{\\mathbb C}=\\mathrm{VNP}_{\\mathbb C}$? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.",
  "definitions": "X has n² independent indeterminates and S_n is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes labeled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, binary +, −, × operation gates, and one output. Its size counts operation gates; intermediate results can feed any number of later gates. Division, comparisons, oracle gates, approximation, and limits of circuits are absent. The output must equal the permanent as a formal polynomial. Circuits may depend on n without a uniform construction algorithm; constants have unit arithmetic cost, with no bit-encoding restriction. VP consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded numbers of variables and total degrees, computed by polynomial-size circuits. VNP consists of polynomial families f_n(x)=Σ_{y∈{0,1}^{p(n)}} g_n(x,y), for some polynomial p and some such polynomial-size, polynomial-degree circuit family g. The witness sum is over Boolean strings even though the coefficients lie in C.",
  "answer_criterion": "Construct the stated circuit family, or prove that the minimum circuit size of the permanent is not bounded by any polynomial in n. A lower bound for every polynomial-size general circuit family suffices. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits, or determinantal representations do not by themselves settle this formulation.",
  "context": "The permanent sums one product for every perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph. Substituting a zero-one adjacency matrix counts perfect matchings. This card asks for an exact symbolic arithmetic computation valid on all complex matrices. The model permits cancellations and unrestricted reuse of intermediate results, so it captures substantially more than enumerating matchings.\n\nThe permanent and determinant have the same permutation products, but the determinant attaches a sign to each one. Determinants have polynomial-size division-free circuits despite their factorially many displayed terms. Thus counting the monomials in the permanent is not a circuit lower bound: the question is whether an equally effective algebraic compression exists for its unsigned sum.\n\nValiant makes this example universal. Every family in VNP reduces to a polynomially larger permanent by substitutions of variables and constants. A polynomial circuit for the permanent would therefore compress every efficient Boolean-witness sum in the definition of VNP. Conversely, separating these classes forces the permanent to escape polynomial circuit size.\n\nImportant partial results restrict how computations are organized. A formula cannot reuse an intermediate result; a constant-depth circuit permits only a fixed number of operation layers. Even proving that the permanent has no small determinant representation would rule out only that representation model. None of these restrictions is part of the circuit model in this card.\n\nRecent lower bounds illustrate both the progress and the gap. Superpolynomial bounds are known at every fixed depth, and new work constructs polynomial maps that evade low-complexity parametrizations. The latter can yield stronger circuit lower bounds if its degree and dimension parameters improve sufficiently. The constructions currently cited do not give the required unrestricted superpolynomial bound.",
